claims: Irish (Gaeilge) is a Goidelic Celtic language.
Irish (Gaeilge) is native to Ireland.
Irish (Gaeilge) is officially recognized in the Republic of Ireland.
Irish (Gaeilge) is officially recognized in Northern Ireland.
Irish (Gaeilge) uses an 18-letter Latin alphabet lacking j, k, q, v, w, x, y, z.
Over 1.8 million people in the 2022 census claimed some ability to speak Irish (Gaeilge).
Daily speakers of Irish (Gaeilge) are concentrated in regions known as the Gaeltacht.
Irish (Gaeilge) is a Celtic language closely related to Scottish Gaelic.
Irish (Gaeilge) is a Celtic language closely related to Manx.
The modern Irish alphabet has 18 letters: a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, l, m, n, o, p, r, s, t, u.
Dia dhuit (pronounced Dee-ah gwit) means Hello (literally 'God to you') in Irish.
Slán (pronounced Slawn) means Goodbye in Irish.
Go raibh maith agat (pronounced Gur rev mah a-gut) means Thank you in Irish.
Fáilte (pronounced Fawl-cha) means Welcome in Irish.
Is mise... (pronounced Iss misha...) means 'I am...' in Irish.
Munster, Connacht, and Ulster.
Gaeilge (pronounced Gwayl-ga) means 'The Irish Language'.
Gaeltacht (pronounced Gwal-tacht) means 'Irish-speaking area'.
Uisce (pronounced Ish-ka) means 'Water' (root of whiskey) in Irish.
Craic (pronounced Crack) means 'Fun/news' (often 'what's the craic?') in Irish.
Roughly 10% of people in Ireland can speak Irish fluently.
About 71,968 daily speakers of Irish (excluding schools) were reported in the 2022 census.
Irish (Gaeilge) was suppressed during centuries of British colonization.
British colonization nearly eradicated Irish (Gaeilge).
Irish (Gaeilge) is used in Gaeltacht areas.
Irish (Gaeilge) is used on road signs.
Irish (Gaeilge) is used in media TG4 and RTÉ Raidió na Gaeltachta.
Irish (Gaeilge) is used as a subject in schools.
